extras.title: Maya peoples · living communities
extras.note: Many distinct Maya peoples, languages and communities persist; this is not a single successor state or a civilisation that ended in 900 AD.

extras.title: Saint-Domingue · French colonial rule
extras.note: French colonial society depended on the enslavement of Africans; its overthrow followed a complex revolution, not a routine administrative transfer.

extras.title: Chimú kingdom / Chimor
extras.note: A regional kingdom centred on Chan Chan, with artistic traditions drawing on earlier north-coast cultures.

extras.title: Spanish colonial Peru
extras.note: Spanish rule developed through conquest and changing jurisdictions; large Indigenous communities and resistance continued.

extras.title: Peru · independent eras
extras.note: Independence was proclaimed in 1821; warfare and royalist resistance continued, including the decisive 1824 campaigns.

extras.title: Quechua-speaking communities
extras.note: Diverse living communities, not an unchanged Inca state; language, identity and local histories are not interchangeable.

extras.title: Caddo communities
extras.note: Distinct confederacies and communities persisted through dispossession and forced removal; historical trade partners are not automatically ancestors.

extras.title: Pueblo peoples · continuing communities
extras.note: Many distinct Pueblo nations share connections to Chaco; no single present-day Pueblo is its sole direct successor.

extras.title: Spanish colonial New Mexico
extras.location: Northern New Spain · Southwestern North America
extras.note: Spanish colonisation was contested; the Pueblo Revolt expelled colonists in 1680, followed by reconquest in the 1690s.

extras.title: East Polynesian voyaging networks
extras.note: Multiple migrations and connected island societies, not one empire or a single founding voyage.

extras.title: Kingdom of Tonga · modern eras
extras.note: Modern consolidation and constitutional government differed from earlier chiefly arrangements; British protection 1900–1970 limited external affairs without annexation.

extras.title: Fijian societies
extras.note: Long histories of distinct island communities precede the modern state and continued through colonial rule.

extras.title: British colonial Fiji
extras.note: The 1874 cession and colonial administration did not end Indigenous Fijian communities; later migration also shaped society.

extras.title: Pohnpei · continuing communities
extras.dates: Island traditions continue · state in FSM since 1979
extras.note: Nan Madol is associated with living chiefly traditions; modern constitutional statehood is distinct from Saudeleur rule.

extras.title: Federated States of Micronesia
extras.note: A federation of four island states with distinct earlier histories; independence developed through constitutional government and the Compact of Free Association.

extras.title: Rapa Nui people · continuing community
extras.location: Rapa Nui / Easter Island and diaspora
extras.note: Rapa Nui people and culture continue beyond the monumental phase; modern administration and Indigenous rights have their own contested history.

extras.title: Chile · independent state
extras.note: The 1888 agreement concerns Rapa Nui and Chile; it is not the founding of Chile or the disappearance of Rapa Nui authority.

extras.title: New Zealand · British colonial era
extras.note: British sovereignty was proclaimed in 1840; the separate colony followed in 1841, and Māori authority and treaty rights remained contested.

maps.title: Mesoamerica & the Caribbean

connections.label: Ancient objects reused
connections.summary: Mexica offerings included an Olmec mask made roughly two millennia earlier.
connections.note: A documented reuse of ancient art, not evidence of a continuous Olmec–Aztec empire.

connections.label: Exchange & artistic connections
connections.summary: Teotihuacan interacted with Maya capitals including Tikal and Copán, with objects and artistic forms crossing regional boundaries.
connections.note: Different cities maintained different relationships; this is not a claim that all Maya lands belonged to Teotihuacan.

connections.label: Communities continue
connections.summary: Maya communities continued long after the Classic-period transformation of their cities.
connections.note: A cultural continuation, not a new state founded in 900 AD.

connections.label: Conquest of Tenochtitlan
connections.summary: Spanish forces and Indigenous allies conquered Tenochtitlan, followed by the development of New Spain.
connections.note: The colonial administration was established in stages; conquest did not end Nahua peoples or all Indigenous resistance.

connections.label: Mexican independence
connections.summary: Mexican independence ended Spanish rule in the core mainland territory represented by this New Spain entry.
connections.note: New Spain extended beyond modern Mexico; later empires, republics and territorial changes followed.

connections.label: French colony
connections.summary: French colonial rule developed in western Hispaniola as Saint-Domingue.
connections.note: This was not all of Hispaniola; the French monarchy later fell while colonial rule continued.

connections.label: Revolution & independence
connections.summary: A revolution against enslavement and French colonial power culminated in Haitian independence in 1804.
connections.note: The conflict involved shifting alliances and foreign intervention; later occupations and political changes are not excluded.

maps.description: Artistic exchange, living Maya communities, conquest in central Mexico and Haiti’s anti-slavery revolution. Separate branches do not imply one regional empire.

maps.title: Andes & Río de la Plata

connections.label: Artistic interaction
connections.summary: Wari artists interacted with Nasca traditions and developed new artistic forms.
connections.note: Interaction and influence do not mean that every Nasca community was replaced by one Wari government.

connections.label: Shared visual traditions
connections.summary: Wari art developed in dialogue with Tiwanaku religious imagery and visual traditions.
connections.note: These were distinct, contemporary powers; the arrow represents cultural interaction, not dynastic succession.

connections.label: North-coast artistic heritage
connections.summary: Chimú artists inherited and reworked earlier Moche cultural and artistic traditions.
connections.note: This is a long artistic relationship across intervening regional developments, not an immediate political handover.

connections.label: Earlier roads & practices
connections.dates: Earlier traditions · adapted by the 15th century
connections.summary: Inca rulers adapted road-building and other practices developed by earlier Wari and Tiwanaku societies.
connections.note: Several centuries and many local histories separate these periods; this is inheritance of practices, not direct state succession.

connections.label: Inca expansion
connections.summary: Inca expansion incorporated the Chimú kingdom into a much larger imperial system.
connections.note: Incorporation did not erase north-coast communities or their craft traditions.

connections.label: Spanish invasion
connections.summary: Spanish invaders exploited the Inca road system during conquest and imposed a new colonial order.
connections.note: The capture of Atahualpa did not instantly conquer the entire Andes; resistance and Indigenous communities continued.

connections.label: Living Andean traditions
connections.summary: Quechua-speaking communities have maintained and transformed traditions associated with the Inca world.
connections.note: Cultural continuation is not continuous imperial sovereignty or a claim that all Quechua speakers share one identity.

connections.label: Peruvian independence
connections.summary: San Martín proclaimed Peruvian independence in Lima in July 1821.
connections.note: A declaration did not end the war immediately or settle every territory.

connections.label: New viceroyalty
connections.summary: The Río de la Plata viceroyalty was created from territories previously administered within the Viceroyalty of Peru.
connections.note: The plotted colonial Argentina frame begins earlier; this arrow specifically concerns the 1776 administrative reorganisation.

connections.label: United Provinces declare independence
connections.summary: The Congress of Tucumán declared the independence of the United Provinces in South America on 9 July 1816.
connections.note: Argentina later developed through conflicts and constitutional changes; the whole former viceroyalty did not become Argentina.

maps.description: Andean cultural interactions, Spanish conquest, colonial reorganisation and selected independence histories. Caral is shown without an unsupported succession arrow.

maps.title: North American communities & changing borders

connections.label: Long-distance exchange
connections.summary: Caddo exchange routes linked their communities with distant centres including Cahokia.
connections.note: Trade connections do not imply shared political government or direct descent from Cahokia.

connections.label: Migration & descendants
connections.summary: People leaving the Chaco region joined communities in several directions, contributing to multiple present-day Pueblo populations.
connections.note: Exact migration routes vary; this does not identify one exclusive heir to Chaco.

connections.label: Colonisation & resistance
connections.summary: Spanish colonisation imposed demands on Pueblo communities, which organised a major revolt in 1680.
connections.note: Pueblo peoples persisted; Spanish control was interrupted and reconquest was gradual and contested.

connections.label: Mexico gains independence
connections.summary: New Mexico became part of independent Mexico after Spanish colonial rule ended.
connections.note: A change in state jurisdiction did not end Pueblo communities or their own institutions.

connections.label: War & territorial cession
connections.summary: The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo ended the U.S.–Mexican War and transferred extensive northern territory to the United States.
connections.note: Mexico continued as an independent state; Indigenous nations were not extinguished by this interstate boundary change.

connections.label: Land cession & forced removal
connections.summary: A Caddo removal treaty with the United States was followed by dispersal and repeated forced removals.
connections.note: This links communities to the state that dispossessed them, not a claim that they ceased to exist or became its predecessor.

maps.description: Caddo exchange networks, Chaco’s descendant communities and later colonial and interstate boundary changes. Indigenous histories continue.

maps.title: Pacific voyaging, communities & modern states

connections.label: Settlement before Tuʻi Tonga
connections.dates: Settlement c. 1100–800 BC · later chiefly societies
connections.summary: Lapita-associated voyagers settled Tonga long before the Tuʻi Tonga chiefly line developed.
connections.note: A settlement and cultural background link, not a claim that the Tuʻi Tonga polity existed in the Bronze Age.

connections.label: Lapita settlement
connections.summary: Lapita-associated voyagers settled Fiji, forming part of its long and changing island histories.
connections.note: Material-culture associations do not make all Pacific peoples one ethnicity or state.

connections.label: Polynesian cultural development
connections.dates: Over many centuries · eastward voyages c. 1000 AD
connections.summary: Polynesian cultures emerged among western island communities before voyages expanded into East Polynesia.
connections.note: This compresses multiple stages through Fiji, Tonga and Samoa; it does not draw a direct Lapita-era voyage to every eastern island.

connections.label: Polynesian settlement
connections.summary: East Polynesian voyagers settled Rapa Nui, where distinctive monumental traditions developed.
connections.note: Dates remain approximate; this does not imply political rule from Tonga.

connections.label: Voyages to Aotearoa
connections.summary: Migrants from East Polynesian islands became the ancestors of Māori communities in Aotearoa.
connections.note: Many voyages and traditions are involved, rather than a single great fleet or an overseas empire.

connections.label: Kingdom consolidation
connections.summary: George Tupou I united the Tongan islands before the 1875 constitution established modern constitutional institutions.
connections.note: A transformation of chiefly and state authority, not an unchanged Tuʻi Tonga empire persisting to the present.

connections.label: Cession & British rule
connections.summary: The 1874 cession established British colonial rule in Fiji.
connections.note: The islands already contained Indigenous societies; colonial administration did not originate or replace their culture.

connections.label: Fijian independence
connections.summary: Fiji became independent from Britain in 1970.
connections.note: Later constitutional changes and coups are included in the broad modern-state entry.

connections.label: Chiefly traditions continue
connections.summary: Nan Madol remains connected to Pohnpei ceremonial traditions and the authority of the Nahnmwarki.
connections.note: Continuing institutions and heritage are distinct from an uninterrupted Saudeleur state.

connections.label: State in a federation
connections.summary: Pohnpei joined the constitutional federation that became the Federated States of Micronesia.
connections.note: The modern federation also includes Chuuk, Kosrae and Yap; centuries of changing colonial administrations lie between Nan Madol and this constitutional transition.

connections.label: A living culture
connections.summary: Rapa Nui people maintain a living relationship with their island and cultural heritage.
connections.note: The end of the selected monumental-phase bar is not the end of Rapa Nui society.

connections.label: 1888 agreement with Chile
connections.summary: The Agreement of Wills formalised Rapa Nui’s incorporation into the Republic of Chile.
connections.note: This state relationship did not end Rapa Nui identity or local titles and authority; its meanings and consequences remain contested.

maps.description: Voyaging and cultural connections alongside selected modern constitutional transitions. These are not branches of a single Pacific empire.

maps.title: Australia & Aotearoa New Zealand

connections.label: First Fleet & colonies
connections.summary: Britain established a convict settlement at Sydney Cove in 1788, followed by expanding and separate colonies.
connections.note: The continent already belonged to many Indigenous nations; British control developed unevenly.

connections.label: Colonisation & dispossession
connections.summary: British settlement disrupted and dispossessed Aboriginal communities while their cultures and resistance continued.
connections.note: The direction marks an encounter with an imposed colonial order, not cultural replacement or extinction.

connections.label: Six colonies federate
connections.summary: Six British colonies united in the Commonwealth of Australia in 1901.
connections.note: Federation did not itself complete constitutional independence or end Indigenous histories.

connections.label: British colonial administration
connections.summary: The British Crown proclaimed sovereignty in 1840 and established New Zealand as a separate colony in 1841.
connections.note: A proclamation of sovereignty is not equivalent to universal Māori consent or immediate control of all territory.

connections.label: Te Tiriti / Treaty of Waitangi
connections.summary: Māori rangatira and the Crown signed a treaty whose Māori and English texts differ in meaning.
connections.note: This is a treaty relationship with disputed sovereignty and obligations, not a merger that ended Māori peoples or authority.

connections.label: Dominion & later autonomy
connections.summary: New Zealand gained Dominion status in 1907, adopted the Statute of Westminster in 1947 and removed remaining British legislative authority in 1986.
connections.note: These were different stages, not one complete independence event in 1907.

maps.description: Continuing Indigenous histories, British colonisation, Australian federation and New Zealand’s treaty and constitutional transitions.

unconnected.reason: Shown as an early Andean urban centre. The reviewed evidence establishes its early urban and ceremonial importance but does not justify a direct political succession arrow to the much later Wari, Tiwanaku or Inca states.
